frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. Aging infrastructure and declining fields constrain its bargaining power over time.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Security Perimeter
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger increases pressure on Algeria's borders and raises the cost of protecting energy corridors. Algiers remains wary of foreign military involvement in the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: External Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting coordinated US, European, and Gulf interest because of its access to critical minerals in the copperbelt. Angola can gain infrastructure and bargaining power, but risks becoming a logistics platform shaped by outside priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure remains important, while oil revenues still dominate fiscal and export earnings. Debt servicing and production volatility limit Luanda's autonomy in allocating resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Transit Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain sensitive because Benin's port and transport corridors are economically tied to regional trade. Border restrictions and diplomatic tensions can disrupt customs revenue and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and energy expansion depends heavily on foreign finance and contractors, particularly from China and international development institutions. This accelerates growth but limits domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has secured greater value retention through local sorting, aggregation, and negotiations with major producers. Weak global diamond demand and synthetic competition nevertheless threaten public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported electricity and scarce water creates infrastructure vulnerabilities despite strong institutions. New generation and water projects will require continued external capital and technical partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Reassertion
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking tighter control over industrial and artisanal gold production, refining, and marketing. This could increase sovereign capture of rents, but opaque licensing and insecurity risk diverting output into illicit networks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's reliance on Russian security cooperation reflects a rejection of Western influence but creates a new external dependency. Conflict-related attacks continue to threaten mines, roads, power assets, and national revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTROL AND TRANSPARENCY
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state leverage over nickel, gold, and rare-earth projects, but limited capital and regulatory capacity leave room for opaque foreign-backed concessions.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA-DRC SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda, eastern DRC armed groups, and cross-border accusations constrain Burundi's trade options and expose transport and mineral corridors to disruption.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, logistics, and maritime security strengthens Cabo Verde's connectivity but creates long-term dependence on external capital and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND FOOD IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains vulnerable to imported fuel, food, and climate shocks, limiting its practical sovereignty despite strong institutions and growing renewable-energy capacity.

highlights: Oil and timber rents remain concentrated

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CONTROL OF RESOURCE CHAINS
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms remain important in mining, timber, construction, and infrastructure, while weak disclosure limits state and public leverage over concession value.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND FAR-NORTH INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insurgency in the Far North, threatens roads, pipelines, plantations, and the state's ability to secure productive regions.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-RESOURCE LINKAGE
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has increased regime protection while raising concerns that mineral access and commercial concessions are exchanged for external military support.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CORRIDOR FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production is divided among state forces, armed groups, and foreign operators, with poor roads and weak customs institutions limiting sovereign capture of resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN OPERATORS
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to state financing, while foreign operators, pipeline arrangements, and opaque fiscal practices constrain N'Djamena's effective control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN BORDER AND EXTERNAL SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war and wider Sahel instability are driving refugee flows, arms trafficking, and military mobilization, placing pressure on border infrastructure and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a persistent sovereignty dispute and complicating Comoros's maritime and migration policy. French economic and security influence remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: External aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, development assistance, and imported fuel and food, limiting its ability to independently control strategic infrastructure and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and regional trading networks retain substantial influence over cobalt, copper, and other strategic minerals. Contract renegotiations and efforts to increase local processing face entrenched commercial and political interests.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23, Rwanda, and other armed networks continues to undermine Kinshasa's control in the east. Regional diplomacy and international security pressure remain central to the country's territorial and resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil dominates export earnings and fiscal capacity, leaving national resource control vulnerable to price swings, production constraints, and foreign technical and financial partners.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and external creditors remain important to transport and public investment. Debt obligations can narrow policy space and increase the strategic value of oil revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value capture
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and farmer support, but multinational traders and volatile global prices still limit national control over cocoa revenues and standards.

frictionVectors.title: Security spillover from Sahel
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in neighboring Sahel states continue to pressure northern border infrastructure and security spending. External partners remain important to surveillance, training, and counterterrorism capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities, including those of the United States, China, France, and Japan, generating revenue and leverage while constraining autonomous security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics infrastructure are closely tied to external capital, especially Chinese-linked projects and Ethiopia's trade flows. Debt exposure and regional competition limit Djibouti's room to impose terms on strategic investors.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic assets, land, and infrastructure. Debt-service pressures constrain Cairo's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: Suez revenues face regional disruption, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved. Egypt is expanding diplomatic and security partnerships to protect water and maritime interests.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Base
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and reliance on foreign technical and capital partners limit domestic control over the hydrocarbon sector. LNG and gas-processing projects remain central to state revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Concentration Risk
frictionVectors.details: State finances and infrastructure investment remain heavily tied to a narrow energy base. Competition among Asian, European, and regional firms shapes access to offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production depends on foreign operators and technical expertise, creating a persistent sovereignty trade-off. Revenue transparency and labor concerns complicate broader investor engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Militarized Maritime Position
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's Red Sea coastline gives it strategic leverage amid regional competition, but sanctions history and strained relations limit infrastructure partnerships. Port development remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African trade corridors, electricity links, finance, and logistics. This dependence narrows room for independent infrastructure and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Concentrated Economic Governance
frictionVectors.details: Political control over land, investment channels, and key commercial interests remains highly centralized. Limited diversification increases exposure to external capital and commodity-market shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation but continues to provoke strategic friction with Egypt and Sudan. Transmission expansion and regional power exports remain vulnerable to diplomatic and security shocks.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and investment needs give China, Gulf states, and Western lenders leverage over infrastructure and economic reforms. Internal conflict and political fragmentation further weaken the state's ability to consolidate resource gains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dominance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign operators remain central to manganese extraction and logistics. Libreville is seeking greater state participation and domestic value addition without destabilizing production.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors around Owendo and mineral rail infrastructure remain vulnerable to external finance, contractors, and commodity-market leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing and weak monitoring continue to threaten Gambian fisheries, food security, and coastal livelihoods. Enforcement capacity remains limited relative to foreign fleets.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, transport, and security ties with Senegal improve connectivity but constrain Banjul's room for independent infrastructure and border policy.

highlights: Gold sector under tighter state scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems and undermine formal state control of gold production. Authorities face pressure to confront politically connected operators and informal networks.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditionality limit policy freedom over mining, energy, and infrastructure spending. Accra is balancing external financial discipline with demands for domestic processing and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor is dominated by large foreign-backed consortia and requires extensive rail and port infrastructure. Guinea's bargaining power is rising, but revenue, technology, and operational control remain heavily external.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and mining-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses resource nationalism to build legitimacy while limiting political accountability. Uncertainty over contracts, local content, and concession access increases friction with investors and communities.

highlights: Fragile state control of extractive waters
Port and fisheries remain strategic vulnerabilities

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and opaque licensing arrangements continue to capture value from Guinea-Bissau's waters. Weak maritime surveillance limits sovereign enforcement and public revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Bissau port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited port capacity and dependence on external contractors constrain trade sovereignty. Regional and foreign actors can exert leverage through transport, customs, and infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Contracts
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and repayment pressure constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese and Gulf-linked infrastructure and logistics interests remain influential, particularly around ports, rail, and industrial corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Resource-Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Plans involving Lamu, northern transport corridors, and prospective minerals face local resistance over land, security, and revenue-sharing concerns. Foreign investment is welcome but risks reinforcing enclave-style development.

highlights: Water Sovereignty Tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide essential revenue but deepen structural dependence on South Africa, which controls the main market and transport links. Pricing, royalties, and project delays remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Phase II Infrastructure and Displacement
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project brings major external financing and infrastructure benefits while generating concerns over compensation, resettlement, and local control of water assets.

highlights: Mining Revival Tests State Bargaining Power

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia relies heavily on foreign mining operators and concession revenues, limiting its leverage over pricing, taxation, and local procurement. Expanding iron-ore activity could improve fiscal capacity but risks reinforcing dependence on commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked operators and investors remain central to port modernization and mineral-transport corridors. Weak infrastructure and governance capacity make transparent contracting and domestic value capture persistent concerns.

highlights: Oil Wealth Divided by Rival Authorities

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and the National Oil Corporation. Shutdown threats and opaque revenue arrangements undermine sovereign management of the hydrocarbon sector.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: External state actors and private security networks retain influence over security zones, bases, and energy infrastructure. This limits Libya's strategic autonomy and complicates efforts to unify fiscal and petroleum institutions.

highlights: Energy and Logistics Gaps Constrain Sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Madagascar captures jobs and royalties but has limited control over processing, pricing, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak transport infrastructure increase reliance on foreign operators and lenders. Port and mining-corridor projects can improve connectivity while concentrating strategic assets outside effective state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERAL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, rare-earth and niobium projects are attracting foreign capital, while Malawi faces pressure to improve contract transparency, local processing and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: FUEL AND FOREIGN-EXCHANGE BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel and constrained foreign exchange limit economic autonomy and leave transport, agriculture and energy infrastructure exposed to external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD CONCESSION CONFRONTATION
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking a larger share of gold revenues and stronger operational control, creating prolonged disputes with international mining companies and raising investment uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel and arms narrows Bamako's diplomatic options while substituting one external dependency for another amid deteriorating relations with Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS DEPENDENCY
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new state revenue and regional influence, but dependence on foreign operators, export infrastructure and Senegalese coordination limits immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND LOGISTICS CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore dependence and foreign-backed rail and port infrastructure expose Mauritania to commodity-price swings and give external investors significant leverage over strategic corridors.

highlights: Ports and finance face strategic pressure

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS IMPLEMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty position over the Chagos Archipelago, but the future of the Diego Garcia base and negotiations with the United Kingdom and United States remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CAPITAL EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: The island's logistics, tourism and financial sectors benefit from Indian, Chinese and Western investment, but this competition can constrain policy autonomy around ports, data and maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of Western Sahara and its phosphate, fisheries and renewable assets remains contested, generating legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and some trading partners.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Tangier Med, renewable-energy projects and planned Atlantic corridors increase Moroccan leverage, while competition among European, Gulf, Chinese and American partners creates balancing pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: LNG development remains exposed to Islamist insurgency, forcing Maputo to rely on foreign military, corporate, and security support. This limits effective sovereign control over the resource frontier.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue and Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and lenders retain substantial influence over project timing, financing, and revenue structures. Domestic expectations for jobs and fiscal benefits continue to outpace delivery.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Investment Terms
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and established uranium production are attracting major foreign investors, creating pressure to balance rapid development with stronger local content and fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen projects depend on large external capital inflows and scarce water and power infrastructure. Sovereignty risks center on whether Namibia retains meaningful ownership and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Recontracting
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral assets while revisiting relationships with Western operators. Reduced technical access and market uncertainty could weaken near-term state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Troop Withdrawal and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The departure or reduction of Western security partners has increased reliance on regional and non-Western arrangements. Persistent militant violence threatens transport corridors, mining zones, and energy infrastructure.

highlights: Gas and Grid Investment Lag Demand

frictionVectors.title: IOC Divestment and Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to capital, technology, and offshore production even as they seek to sell selected onshore assets. Regulatory reform has improved the framework but has not eliminated foreign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Export Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, crude theft, and weak evacuation infrastructure continue to suppress output and fiscal receipts. Reliance on imported refined products also exposes national energy security to external price and supply shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to armed groups in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate sustained diplomatic pressure over mineral traceability and cross-border sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships and Aid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda converts disciplined security institutions into diplomatic and commercial influence, including external peacekeeping partnerships. Continued reliance on aid, investment, and international security contracts constrains full economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore petroleum uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest in the joint development zone with Nigeria offers potential revenue but leaves São Tomé dependent on larger partners and exposed to disputes over commercial terms.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects rely heavily on foreign financing and technical assistance, limiting domestic bargaining power despite the country's strategic location.

highlights: New oil and gas revenues reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Production from Sangomar and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens state finances, but foreign operators, financing structures, and revenue-management rules remain central to the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, power, and digital projects attract Gulf, Chinese, European, and Turkish capital, creating opportunities while raising concerns over debt exposure and control of critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign naval cooperation, surveillance support, and donor financing to secure its extensive maritime zone against piracy, trafficking, and illegal fishing.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and coastal asset exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign ownership and investment dominate tourism and major infrastructure, creating growth but leaving land, water, and coastal resilience policy vulnerable to external commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral logistics
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated rail and port systems provide export income, but foreign capital and logistics arrangements can constrain domestic value capture and policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Interest in rutile, bauxite, gold, and emerging battery-mineral prospects is increasing competition among investors while stressing licensing transparency, environmental safeguards, and local-content rules.

highlights: Offshore oil ambitions meet weak capacity
Ports remain instruments of regional rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Offshore petroleum sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: New exploration and licensing efforts promise revenue but depend on foreign companies, security guarantees, and contested federal-state arrangements, creating risks of opaque contracts and fragmented control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed port competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, China, and neighboring countries compete for influence through port, military, and logistics projects, linking infrastructure access to Somalia's broader security and sovereignty struggles.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Grid and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, rail failures, and congested ports constrain sovereign control over mineral exports and increase reliance on private and foreign infrastructure capital.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group mineral access, while Pretoria seeks local beneficiation without deterring investment.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to regional war
External security and finance remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: Sudan pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production, revenue, and transit access vulnerable to armed disruption and bargaining by external actors.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control over oil rents
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, elite competition, and foreign oil operators limit transparent national control of petroleum revenues and infrastructure.

highlights: War fragments gold and oil governance
Ports and corridors are geopolitical prizes

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war-finance networks
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and foreign-linked trading networks capture or monetize gold flows, undermining state ownership and formal revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access competition
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated military, logistics, and maritime interests attract rival external powers, making infrastructure access part of the wider conflict economy.

highlights: LNG and rail corridors reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and local content
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over gas development seek greater state participation, revenue certainty, and domestic processing while international firms retain capital and technical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and logistics projects can expand Tanzania's regional leverage but may create long-term dependence on external finance, contractors, and operating standards.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign shipping, logistics, and infrastructure capital is central to Lomé's growth, creating exposure to outside influence over a strategically important Gulf of Guinea gateway.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate beneficiation gap
frictionVectors.details: The state retains a major role in phosphate resources, but limited domestic processing and dependence on external markets constrain value capture and industrial sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European support for migration control and budget stability gives Brussels significant influence over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance remains strong against perceived externalization of European border control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and declining phosphate performance, limiting fiscal autonomy and increasing dependence on external financing and investment.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline strengthens Uganda's prospective export capacity but leaves the project exposed to Western environmental, sanctions, and financing pressure. Tanzania's transit role also limits Uganda's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and growing foreign interest in gold, copper, and other minerals are expanding Uganda's options while raising concerns over opaque contracts and limited domestic value capture.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Fiscal Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater domestic processing, tax enforcement, and state participation in copper while remaining dependent on foreign mining capital and commodity revenues. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors is increasing bargaining leverage but also contract pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and vulnerable export corridors constrain mining expansion and national revenue. Reliance on regional power imports and multiple transit routes exposes Zambia to infrastructure and political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Critical-Mineral Control
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and local-processing demands to capture more value from lithium and other minerals, but Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in extraction and refining. Weak transparency and limited domestic capital constrain effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent currency instability, sanctions-related constraints, and dependence on gold and mineral receipts reduce policy autonomy. External investors can negotiate from a position of strength because the state needs foreign exchange and infrastructure finance.
